utterances.text: And then number -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it -- is it necessary for me to comment or to provide you my opinion or was I just supposed to read it out so that it gets interpreted? Perhaps it might be of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, please, then, if you want to give me your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'll be very brief. On the basis of this one way conclude that the command of the Pristina Corps has jurisdiction over its own forces and the MUP staff over its own forces, so they have an additional task to regulate all other issues regarding the engagement with their own orders. This is quite unambiguous. As far as I'm concerned, as a soldier, for me, this is quite unambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When -- when at the Supreme Command Staff level did you as a group become aware that there was a problem regarding the order for subordination of the MUP, do you recall? When did you realise that it wasn't happening as it was supposed to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we at the Supreme Command Staff were a group, I want to tell you that we were a well-organized group. We had our organization, the establishment, we did things in a particular sequence; and secondly, I don't remember any special or dramatic developments at the collegium or the evening briefing relating to this issue. It is possible that somebody had more or less knowledge of that, but we as a group, as you termed us, we did not receive special information regarding this. I know that there were some isolated complaints by the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you did -- whenever it was that you became aware that there was some problem about that subordination of the MUP, did the Supreme Command Staff take any steps to try and address it; and if so, what were those?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the chief of the Supreme Command Staff on at least one occasion in early May informed the supreme commander, President Milosevic, about that one morning. Now, I don't know what was done subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go back to 3D670 for just a minute, this is the original order regarding subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you told us when you were here last time at page 16984 and 16985 that you had seen this order by President Milosevic, but that the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff did not send this or any other to Minister Stojiljkovic. No orders were sent to the minister of interior, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the military cabinet sent it, but the Supreme Command Staff did not send this or any other order to the Ministry of the Interior. I know that for sure because they were not part of our chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But item number 3 in that order says the: "Chief of the Supreme Command Staff will send his request to the civilian government organs and other defence bodies ..." So did the Supreme Command Staff send requests to the Ministry of the Interior or any other government organs in connection with subordinating the MUP, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know, but your question is not unambiguous. Let me first tell you that the Supreme Command Staff issued several documents to the authorities, the federal defence minister, the government, the finance minister, the justice minister, and others within its purview pursuant to this authorisation in paragraph 3. But no document, as far as I know, was sent to the defence ministry, or rather, to the Ministry of the Interior or the Federal Ministry of the Interior regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why was that? Because the army viewed it did not have the authority to send that to the Ministry of the Interior, because it seems that by not doing so General Ojdanic is disobeying the order of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. He complied with the order issued by President Milosevic and he complied with what he was supposed to do as the Chief of Staff and what the army was supposed to do. But apparently somebody else was made responsible for this other system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't understand that. Where -- how do you reach that conclusion, somebody else was made responsible for that? Doesn't this direct General Ojdanic to send a request to the government organs and wouldn't that include the Ministry of Interior? Or is that not a civilian government organ?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we both know that it was a civilian government organ, and we also know that this was the organ of the Republic of Serbia. All the other things were done, so what -- why would the chief of the Supreme Command Staff send a request to the republican ministry or to the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia to do anything with or about MUP? I would expect - and I indeed expected - that this order would be sent, forwarded, to the presidents of Yugoslavia and of Serbia [as interpreted] and to the relevant ministries outside of the military, including the MUP, the part that had to do with MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, 49, 19, I believe the witness says the president of Yugoslavia and the prime ministers of the federal government and the Government of Serbia, not the presidents of Serbia. It can be checked on the audio as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Line 19. The witness said: To the president of Yugoslavia, the prime minister of the federal government, and the prime minister of Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not the president of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note, General, that you were nodding your head affirmatively to that; that was correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and you understood me. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I'm not clear then, if this is all about the MUP being resubordinated or subordinated to the army, isn't the Ministry of the Interior the most important and most pertinent and most likely civilian government organ that needs to know about it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you're trying to switch the arguments here. Why would the Supreme Command Staff, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff inform the Ministry of the Interior that the supreme commander had ordered him something? This is not how things are done. This is not the chain of command within an army or in a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But isn't that what this order directs him to do? Isn't President Milosevic here telling General Ojdanic to send his request - and I take it that would be a request for MUP units to be subordinated to the army for combat operations - isn't that what he's supposed to do pursuant to this document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Why would President Milosevic then make this order and then try to persuade the chief of the Supreme Command to send an order to the Ministry of the Interior or some other organ for its resubordination? That's not how it was, that's not how it is. It's absolutely crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I must need new glasses. I don't see how that's clear. Isn't that what item 3 says? It doesn't say send an order, it says send a request. I agree with you about that distinction, but General Ojdanic didn't send a request, did he?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic did send a certain number of requests to other organs --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But not to the --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- But he decided that they should be sent, not to the MUP, he didn't send any such requests to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know -- do you know whether during the war General Ojdanic had communications, either written or face-to-face, or telephonic conversations with the minister of the interior, Mr. Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I don't know whether he had any face-to-face contacts with him, as far as I can remember no. As far as any telephonic contacts, I can't tell you. I don't know whether they had any correspondence, but if yes that was not through the Supreme Command Staff, so I don't know. And I can give you my personal opinion, they did not, they were not in contact, but somebody would know that. General Ojdanic would boast to somebody or other that he had called the minister of the interior and talked to him about something, he would report that to us at the briefing. But that was not the case, and I also know that the minister never called him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, have I rightly understood that you regard this order as having nothing to do with either the MUP of the federal republic or the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mention the federal ministry of the interior in the context of paragraph 3, I only mentioned the ministry of the republic in the context of the question that was asked of me by Mr. Hannis. I know that several documents were sent to the Federal Ministry of the Interior during the war and that we received several such documents from them of different nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said earlier that no document as far as you know was sent to the Ministry of the Interior or the Federal Ministry of the Interior regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I mentioned the federal MUP regarding this issue, then that is the case. So in this regard, the Chief of Staff did not get in contact with the MUP. He did on some other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say that he did contact the federal defence minister -- well, it's difficult to see what he's got to do with units and organs of the interior. He issued it to the finance minister, the justice minister. So what is all this about? What is this document about if these are the people that General Ojdanic sends the request to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember several such things at the federal level, the federal ministries. For instance, there was this constant problem regarding the procurement of certain things that needed to be procured, lack of foreign exchange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, let me interrupt you there. The wording of this order - please let's not forget that - is: "Pursuant to Article 17 of the Law on Defence units and organs of the interior are to be resubordinated to the Yugoslav Army." Now, what is meant there by "units and organs of the interior"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the units of the interior in the area of combat operations that carry out joint combat actions. So we're not talking about public law and order, we're not talking about fire-fighting units, and any other units of the MUP, but just those units that engage in combat or may be used in combat together with the Army of Yugoslavia or under its command in a certain area over a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you give this quite a restricted meaning. Now, tell me what units and organs fall within this description.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Units that may engage in combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Name them. Tell us what these are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, the police detachment, police companies, special units, things like that that would be used to carry out a specific task or mission. This is clearly stipulated in Article 7 [as interpreted] of the Law on Defence, how and under which circumstances this can be done, this resubordination can be done, the resubordination of MUP to the Army of Yugoslavia, and the time-period is specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness said Article 17, 53, 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look at paragraph 3 of this order, Mr. Curcin, which refers to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff sending requests. What do you understand to be meant by requests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is rather broadly termed, it could be the minister of defence, so that civilian defence and civilian protection units can be resubordinated or something else in that area, it could be prime minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, you've just told me that the document doesn't deal with civilian defence. You've given a very restricted interpretation of the police units to which this would refer. I've asked you which units and organs and you've told me. Now, why should the requests not relate to these units and organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was very precise. In paragraph 1 there is a reference to the units and organs of the interior, of internal affairs, and you told me -- you asked me about paragraph 3, which requests, what kind of requests could be addressed to civilian authorities, and I gave as one example the minister of defence, the minister of finance, the federal prime minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, just bear with me a moment. You specified the units of the interior and you said, for instance, the police detachment, police companies, special units, things like that that could be used to carry out a specific task or mission and this is clearly stipulated in Article 17 of the Law on Defence. Now, is it not reasonable to assume that paragraph 3 which talks about the requests is about requests relating to these units and organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there's no way I could understand it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, then that's a matter for us then in due course. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you talked about the interior organs that could be used for combat operations, isn't it a fact that in 1999 the only significant MUP combat components were in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia rather than the federal MUP? Federal MUP didn't have any significant number of combat units or personnel, did it, not in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, when you were here last time, asked you whether it was correct that not a single combat report ever reported of problems undertaking any combat action arising out of any refusal of the MUP to obey or undertake VJ orders for that operation, and you said: "Yes, you're right." But you've -- we've seen earlier in Exhibit P1459, General Pavkovic mentioned problems with the MUP until allegedly engaging in crimes against the civilian population, right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to answer because I've said I hadn't seen this act.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Based on what you said to Mr. Ivetic, would you agree with me, then, there really wasn't any need for formal subordination of the MUP if they were working so well in coordinating with the VJ that there was never a single reported problem regarding combat operations carried out jointly?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with it completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement paragraph 44 that you had known General Ojdanic for a long time, you worked directly with him, and you were in his immediate vicinity all the time. But you weren't with him during times when he went to meet with the supreme commander, President Milosevic, correct? You didn't attend any of their meetings, their daily meetings, did you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend any of his meetings with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not he met with any other high-ranking civilians in the government during the war time-period, in particular President Milutinovic or Mr. Sainovic? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if General Ojdanic had any standard procedure in his office about transcribing or having transcribed telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the word "transcribed."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, for example, either someone sitting in during a conference call and typing up what was said during the conversation or a tape-recording made of the telephone call and then typed up by someone else later. Do you know if he ever did that during the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know a civilian employee for the VJ, a typist called Biljana Popovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What office did she work in?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember which office, I know it was on the ground floor of the General Staff, but she was not to the best of my recollection at the command post, at least I didn't see her there. But she was not part of his office, and when I went to see him I never saw her.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about an English-language interpreter named Zorica Stosic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person. I know Vesna Jankovic, though, the woman Clark also got to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. General, one last document I want to ask you a few questions about is 3D695. I only have it in the Serbian language and I have a hard copy, I guess I'll give that to you. I just want to ask you a few questions about what this is and what you might know about how it was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I'm just going to ask foundational questions based on what we discussed before, I think there's no problem in being in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's already been acknowledged by Mr. Visnjic, and as far as I can tell nothing that's been said about this today needed private session, although it was probably wise to do it that way. So I propose that that material from earlier today be simply made part of the public record. There's no aspect of it that was confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps we shouldn't show it on the e-court display, just out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that would satisfy the -- any concern that might be had by the producers of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, that's been described to me as the war diary for the Supreme Command Staff during the war. Now you have had a chance to look at it a little bit, would you -- am I right about that or --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's volume 1, notebook 1, the first of four of the war diary of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And from my limited ability to read Cyrillic, it appeared that these were daily entries I think beginning on the 23rd of March through sometime in late June 1999, and the daily entries were usually signed by someone, various generals who we've seen here as members of the Supreme Command Staff. I would direct you to I think what's page number 31 in your hard copy. There's an entry with what appears to be your name at the bottom. Is that it on the left?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was signed by the leader of the operations team on duty in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to ask you what this document is and how was it maintained and how was it kept and where -- where would it have been since the end of the war when it was finalised?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer the first part of the question. It was kept in keeping with the instructions for the work of commands and staffs stipulating exactly what is entered into a war diary. I designated two officers at the colonel level who made entries based on requests and orders, and what is entered here are all the major orders, developments, and everything that was relevant to the Supreme Command Staff and the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was it -- how was it decided who made the entry for a particular day? Because I see several different names, at least six or seven different names. Was it just a rotating duty among you all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the signing. I'm talking about both the signing and about making entries, the writing. There were only two colonels who made entries, they were from the first administration and I designated them. The signatures were put by leaders of the operations team on duty that took turns every five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the two colonels who made those entries, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Navy Captain Karlicic, and I believe Colonel Zoran Srbulovic because there were another two colonels whom I designated for other work. I believe these were in charge of the war diary, Navy Captain Karlicic, therefore, and Colonel Zoran Srbulovic, who was in charge of the 2nd Army, who was a clerk for the 3rd Army, that is. And as far as I remember, Colonel Paskas and Colonel Mucibabic were in charge of evening briefings, on making notes for evening briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we've heard evidence from Mr. Mucibabic about that. Thank you. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A couple of matters came up in the cross that were not totally anticipated that I think I can shed some light on and be helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's a novel approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I thought I would try a different way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me what these are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One has to do with the 17th April suggestions document of General Pavkovic that was talked about at length; the other has to do with this issue of resubordination that was also talked about at length, both of which have relevance to my client and that's why I want to go into them. There's a couple of documents that I can deal with that I think will shed some light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any problem with that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would find it helpful to hear more on both these subjects, so please continue, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, we've noticed of course as we looked at these various orders and documents we look at, frequently you see at the beginning of that document a reference to some other document that it is referred to an order from the Supreme Command or an order from the 3rd Army or it's referring to something. So one of the things I want to do with you is connected a few documents here so that maybe we can understand them just a little bit better. I'd like you first to take a look at 4D220, and that will come up on your screen just a moment. You've been looking today at the order by President Milosevic on resubordination of the MUP. This is an order on the same day signed by General Ojdanic, apparently an effort to implement the order of President Milosevic. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, it says that right in the first paragraph. It says: "Pursuant to the order of the President of the FRY." And the first thing I want you to notice is where it was sent to, to the commands of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army and the navy and to the office. What is the office?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the office of the chief of Supreme Command Staff. One copy was delivered to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And then the other thing I want us to just make a note of, there's a number on this document up at the top, it's 01/2024-1. And as we remember that number, let's go now to 4D420. Now, I think you'll recall that the orders of Milosevic and Ojdanic on MUP resubordination were dated the 18th of April. You're looking now at a document that is dated the 20th of April, and this is a document from General Pavkovic. And what I'm interested in is paragraph 3 of that document right now. And apparently what General Pavkovic says there, first of all, you notice he refers to the Ojdanic document we just looked at 01/2024-1 dated 18 April. What General Pavkovic says, if you're really serious about this resubordination business, you should forward this to the minister of the interior, I assume it is, of the Republic of Serbia so that he can undertake the measures within his competence and transmit the order to the, probably, appropriate organs, although the translation is not clear in that regard. Is that pretty much what that says?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still haven't got to that part where it says you seriously mean, are you going to refer me to a specific paragraph so we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 is what I'm -- I asked you to look at paragraph 3. Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what is it that General Pavkovic is suggesting there? He's suggesting that this resubordination needs to be forwarded to some other people, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The translation is not totally clear, and I don't know if we can get it clear. It says that kindly forward it to the minister, something, of the Republic of Serbia. Can you read it? Which minister does he suggest it be forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, one cannot make out the whole word in my copy, not even the word minister is quite clear, let alone the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks like it says "i ministru vr" or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We just lost the page. If we can make that one bigger that may help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks like there's a VR or something like that there. Do you have any idea what that means?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you can't read it? Some people say it's VP some people say it's RP do any of these make any sense to you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mean anything; if you can help me, I'll be glad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told that UP would stand for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is V unlike the first letter after the digit 3 in paragraph 3, it's clear that this one is V, and there is a clear difference between the two letters. The U in the -- at the beginning of the first line and the V at the beginning of the fourth line. And the second letter is really illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, does it make sense to you that what General Pavkovic would be saying here if he's talking about resubordination of units and organs of the Ministry of the Interior, that he would suggest that that ought to be sent to the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to -- let's go to the first page of this document now. Now, you'll recall that meeting where General Ojdanic suggested that you look into the telegram, that's 3D589, the briefing, paragraph 6, where he suggests that you look into the telegram and you said that was probably the telegram of the 17th of April that you had testified so much about. Did you do that? Did you look into that to find out what had happened with that telegram to see when it was received, when it was sent, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the circumstances that were mentioned by Mr. Hannis in his question, but he just asked me briefly about the beginning and he didn't go on into it any further. Because it's only in that context that I discussed it, when Mr. Hannis mentioned tasks or assignments from the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 18th of April, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, he showed you that meeting from the 18th where one of the tasks was for you to find out when that was sent and when it was received. My question is: Did you do that? Did you carry out that task? Did you find out when that telegram was sent and when it was received?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I tried, I did my very best. I established clearly that it was sent immediately, it was sent on time, and the time is indicated, the time of transmission is indicated. But unfortunately I couldn't accomplish my task fully and report to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff as to when it was delivered because it hasn't -- it hadn't been delivered by that morning. The commander was not at the command post and the telegram just wandered from one place to another among the places where he could be, and he ended up not being delivered by the time that was indicated as commencement of attack. Later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- The liaison officer tried to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a hard copy of this document, 4D420, that will help you. We're going to have to look at some of the language of it here in a minute. Do you remember the number of that 17 April document, the telegram from General Ojdanic with the suggestions as being 01/1965-1, do you remember that being the designation of that document? We can look at it if you don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it. I don't remember such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look very quickly at that document then just so we all know that, it's P1487, and then we'll have to bring the other one right back. Okay. There it is, and you see the number is 01/1965-1, right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now we'll go back to 4D420 again. And now I'll direct your attention to paragraph 2. Now, there's a mystery here which we probably won't solve, but paragraph 2 says: "With respect to the delivery of the telegram strictly confidential number 01/1965-1," which we just saw, "dated 14 April 1999," that is the wrong date, isn't it? One of them is wrong. Either the first one should have been 14 April or this one should have said 17 April, but it does say "suggestions." And then he says: "I report as follows. It arrived at 0025 hours on the 18th of April at Prolom Banja, forwarded at 105 to Prekovce village which is 36 kilometres from Pristina, and finally delivered to the commander of the 3rd Army at 0715 hours on the 19th of April, right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph talks about the problems with delivery and why it was not possible to get to him immediately because he was moving and communications weren't as perfect as they might have been, right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here. I don't know if it's right, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now we can go back to paragraph 1 and learn something, I think, about the genesis of this whole proposition. General Pavkovic points out in that paragraph that this whole operation was done at the command of the supreme commander, who on the 12th of April ordered that within the next seven days this operation should be carried out by the JSO and the SAJ of the MUP and that units of the Yugoslav Army were to be engaged basically in a supporting role. He sets that out to explain why he couldn't follow the suggestions of General Ojdanic because it was a MUP operation, planned and organized by MUP and the MUP command, and that the VJ units were there just to carry out some blocking arrangements. You see that in paragraph 1, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, but that quite simply is not correct because it's on the 19th of April that he got the telegram and this was supposed to happen on the 18th of April. In paragraph 2, the last bit says that it was delivered at 7.15 on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right, he says he didn't get it until after the operation had been carried out, but that it was a MUP operation and he couldn't have done anything about it anyhow, right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't attend that meeting or that part of the meeting on the 12th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go back to paragraph 3 appeared look at the second paragraph in paragraph 3, General Pavkovic says: "It was not possible to have any useful influence on halting Operation Rugovo on this basis." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer wasn't picked up by the interpreter. Can you answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreter please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "correct," although I did not manage to read paragraph 3 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please take time to read as much as you want because my next question kind of requires that you know the document. I suggest to you that there's nothing in this document talking about any kind of a Joint Command or that this was any kind of a Joint Command operation, is there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned the words "Joint Command" in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the words aren't in it, are they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first glance, as I skim through the document, I do not see "Joint Command" mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, the logical conclusion from reading paragraph 1 is that this was primarily a MUP operation for which the VJ had a very minor supporting role, to prevent a spill over of forces into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the 2nd Army was involved in closing off axes leading to the Republic of Montenegro, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure that I can phrase this any better than Mr. Ackerman already did, so I am going to repeat his words. I think that a question comes from the cross-examination that did not appear in the direct examination, and it has to do with the armed non-Siptar population. I have one question for General Curcin in relation to that, or rather, I am seeking clarification and it is important as far as my client is concerned and for our defence case in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Carry on, please, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, before I put my question I would like to display on e-court P1878.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Curcin, or rather, General, I beg your pardon. You have already looked at paragraph 2 and commented on it where this unarmed Siptar population is referred to. I would like to ask you when we see the document in Serbian, we would like to have paragraph 5 displayed, I think it's page 3, and it is entitled "tasks." We have it in English. Could we please see it in Serbian as well, a page before that. Tasks of units, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. In these tasks do you see anywhere that a specific order is being issued to a unit or structure or component of the unarmed Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, I just see 5.1. I do not see what follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You've seen 5.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have the second page displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are talking about the unarmed Siptar population -- we are talking about the armed Siptar population, I am sorry, I seem to be changing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we're talking about the armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, Your Honour. I seem to have turned it the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have you had a look at all of paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before you we heard testimony here that the civil defence amounted to 9.000. We'll see later on during the defence case perhaps there was even more. General Farkas testified about this, when he was in the Ministry of Defence. In this order is there a concrete task issued to any part of a unit, any unit, any part of this armed non-Siptar population and is there a specific determination as to what communication, what facility, and what task they have, what they should do?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this, quite simply, does not exist in this task issued to concrete units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So we can say, we can agree, that this is just something that has nothing to do with the specific tasks issued to a specific unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. That's a matter for the Tribunal to determine in due course by analysing all the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That would be it. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, anything arising out of any of that further cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness please be shown 3D670.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, before that, General, may I ask you the following. Can you tell me who are the subjects of defence according to the Law on Defence, if you can recall that readily? Or let's have a look. You cannot remember?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really hope you could help me because the laws have been changed. I have been in retirement for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not deal with it at such length.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see 3D -- no, sorry, P985, that is the Law on Defence, Article 2. Articles 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you better repeat the question, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, General, can you tell us who, according to the Law on Defence, are the subjects of defence? The law is from 1994.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of Article 2 of the Law on Defence, it is clear that in addition to the Army of Yugoslavia, the subjects of defence are citizens, federal organs and organizations, local self government, and companies whose activity, or rather, companies that are engaged in certain activity, and other legal entities here and after referred to as citizens, state organs, companies, and other legal entities. They and the Army of Yugoslavia shall exercise their rights and responsibilities in the defence of the country in the times of peace and war in accordance with the law and other federal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we have a look at Article 17 of the Law on Defence, that is the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me then, Article 17 of the Law on Defence, in addition to the units and organs of internal affairs, does it refer to any other organs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is clearly stated in this paragraph that this only pertains to organs of the interior, units and organs of the interior, of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at 3D670, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, General, when you read paragraph 3 of this order, can you tell me whether you can link this up with Article 17 of the Law on Defence?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not directly. Actually, what is written here is that the chief of the staff will send his request to the civilian government organs and other defence bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And if I'm right, during your examination by Mr. Hannis and the questions put to you by Judge Bonomy, your evidence was that the Chief of General Staff indeed did address requests to other subjects of defence, irrespective of Article 17?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could the witness please be shown 3D694. Your Honour, before I move on to that, again I have a document that is not on my list. My -- this submitted through the bar table, but perhaps I should deal with this in writing not to make it too extensive at this point in time, perhaps I should deal with it in writing so it doesn't lead to further re-examination. So could 3D694 be shown to the witness now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, are you aware of that document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us briefly what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a tour and control towards the end of May, between the 23rd and 26th in the Pristina Corps of the 3rd Army, voluminous notes were made and the late General Ljubisa Velickovic as head of that team compiled this document and submitted it to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff for his signature, and he sent it to the commander of the 3rd Army. It briefly states that a team of the Supreme Command Staff tour the command and several units and establish many positive things, but also noted quite a few problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us not be too extensive. General, is one of the problems referred to in this report the fact that the MUP units were not resubordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what was the other document you were contemplating?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D1087.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, the suggestion made was that Mr. Visnjic would deal with this in writing to avoid further examination. If this document is going to be presented and then lead to questions on your part, we should deal with it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. It's on his list on his motion filed today to add exhibits, and I don't know off the top of my head what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we just leave it then and deal with it through the written motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm agreeable either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll leave it as it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The weather for your unexpected weekend in The Hague was not too bad, Mr. Curcin. We're sorry, obviously, that you had to delay your return, but that now completes your evidence. We're grateful to you for coming to give evidence, and you may now leave the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall break now, and I assume we'll resume with Mr. Radinovic at 6.00. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I with your leave before Mr. Visnjic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Raise a preliminary issue in respect to this witness. We had filed an objection to the report and part of the objection was that we were receiving or had not received certain sources that were referred to in the footnotes. Since then, starting from, I think, Friday of last week and continuing until yesterday, we have begun receiving not all but many of these sources, many of them in -- not translated into English. That puts us in a serious difficulty in trying to confirm the accuracy of these citations, and in the circumstances we may be -- we may need, and it seems as if at this point we do need to ask the Court, firstly, if the cross-examination could be postponed for a day. And it is possible, although I don't expect so and I hope not, that we may have to apply for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of the sort of problem that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to no documents provided, at footnote 40, footnote 54, footnote 62, and it goes on and on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just say what was the one you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Footnote 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 40. And the second one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that still part of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which section? Are you referring to 40 or 52?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Footnote 54, is that section of the report still included?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, it is. Well, 54, you did say 54?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have all the collegium minutes that are relevant for this case. What was the third one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 54 is a general reference to collegium minutes. That one is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. What's the next one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 62. It must be a certain specific elements of that that you're talking about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For example, the 21st of March, 1999, presumably is a document, and I think there are two or three others in this footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that each of these footnotes relates to documents that you've asked for and have not received?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We submitted that the factual parts of the report, the parts that he says he bases his views on should be sourced and -- as we did with the experts that we submitted. And in fairness to the Defence, they sought to do so, but they have not submitted all. And on top of that some that have been submitted are in B/C/S, although we are trying with language assistants to see if we could look over those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are right, of course, Mr. Stamp that if something that the expert says depends on a matter of fact, then the fact has to be proved. And if Mr. Visnjic has chosen not to prove it, you might find that that's to your advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, what we shall do at this stage at least is proceed to hear the examination-in-chief of Mr. Radinovic, and you can let us know when it comes your turn to cross-examine what the state of play is, and we would expect to be told specifically what is the material that you consider ought to be in your hands and translated at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer or should I proceed with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should tell us his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His full name is Radovan Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this examination-in-chief will be relatively brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be asked, I gather, a limited number of questions by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I start with the questions for General Radinovic, I would like to say that his military expert report was admitted into evidence as 3D1116, that his CV is in e-court as 3D1069, both the documents are in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, they are not admitted into evidence until you ask him to tell us something about them and their accuracy, and then no doubt that hurdle will be overcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in July 2007 you wrote a report with the title: "Military expertise, analysis of the control competence of General Dragoljub Ojdanic in the war in Kosovo and Metohija in 1988 [as interpreted] /1999"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Have you reviewed that report after that and is it the case that you found certain errors in it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Have you specified those errors in a document written yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that most of these errors relate to more specific indications that are to be found in footnotes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are other errors as well, but most of them are as you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document headed: "Corrigendum to the report" was introduced into e-court under number 3D1123. In order not to repeat every correction into the record, I believe this way of proceeding would be more useful. I also suggest that in addition -- in addition to the report, with your leave of course, this corrigendum be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment to look at it --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Visnjic. Should we be substituting the existing footnote with these ones? Is that how it operates?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Essentially, yes, Your Honours. Because the greatest part of these corrections are in fact a better specification of documents or more precise description of things contained already in previous documents. And some of them are based on similar documents already existing in e-court. We wanted to minimise the number of documents and use primarily those that are already in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Mr. Stamp, to us simply taking the corrigendum as read and making the appropriate substitutions of footnotes in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can proceed on the basis you've indicated, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one addition to make concerning footnote 206. It's a document that Mr. Ackerman used in the courtroom half an hour ago. I did not have the reference then, but I can say now that the document in footnote 206 is document 4D420 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, the witness has confirmed to me that the military expert report before you is his report, and I have no questions to ask of him. All that the Defence wanted to hear from the witness is stated in the report; therefore, I suggest that his report, his CV, and the corrigendum be admitted into evidence as Defence exhibits for the accused Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radinovic, since we concentrated there on the errors rather than the accuracies in this report, can you confirm that subject to the corrigendum or the corrigenda listed, that this is an accurate report of your findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are there Defence counsel who intend to cross-examine the witness? None -- oh, there are. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can proceed this afternoon, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I mentioned in communication with the Chamber that I might have some questions but I wouldn't be ready until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but at the moment do you know whether you're likely to cross-examine or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right now I know that I have one question, but by tomorrow I may have 74, who knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I assume you will have no objection to Mr. Ivetic preceding you. Mr. Ivetic, are you happy about that, since if there's any prejudice arises you know that you'll be given an opportunity to rectify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that. I was just hoping to be able to shorten some of my questions since I have quite a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give us the short version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll try and do it on the go. Can I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, as you know my name is Dan Ivetic and I represent Sreten Lukic. I have a couple of areas that I would like to explore with you relating to items contained in your report, the military expert report that you have just verified with Mr. Visnjic. The first area that I would like to question you on relates to your opinions relating to 1998 activities in Kosovo and Metohija, specifically paragraph 90 of your report you state that with respect to anti-terrorist actions undertaken in 1998: "Striving to discharge the mission while avoiding NATO's military engagement, the Serbian and Yugoslav leadership opted for combining police and military action without declaring a state of war or emergency. Such a political decision predetermined that the crucial and leading role of the operation should be played by the police forces and the police leadership." This is your opinion or conclusion from viewing events in 1998 as an outsider with respect to the anti-terrorist actions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a complete outsider. I was a citizen of that state who followed, to the extent possible, all those events, but I was not an insider either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you were not among the persons making the decisions about the use of forces in the anti-terrorist actions and you were not involved in the planning of any of the anti-terrorist actions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, for the moment I would like to focus on the role of the police, if we may. Is it your opinion that the use of the MUP of Serbia in anti-terrorist actions in 1998 was essentially a political decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's the way I understood your conclusion, then you didn't quite understand. Engagement of defence forces is certainly a political decision because appropriate, competent state authorities make the decision to engage them, that's one. Second, the police forces, that is, security forces, also have to respond to challenges on the spot; that means that whenever there occurred activities of the terrorist forces, the forces of the Ministry of the Interior responded to such actions so that by engaging defence forces in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 a political decision was made, that political decision was necessary. And all those forces had the only task to provide defence and security for the state territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say that those forces had the only task to provide defence and security for the state territory. I'd like to delve into that in some detail. First of all, with respect to the MUP Serbia, based upon your review, research, and preparation of this report, would you agree with me that they are duty-bound not only to protect the territory but to protect, uphold, and enforce the laws of Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And specifically with respect to terrorism, I'm sure you're aware that the act of terrorism is considered a commission of a criminal act by the relevant laws, such as the [B/C/S spoken]. In English that's the criminal code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Article 15, section 125.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a question, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm inclined to take your word for it, but I don't have the law before me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down and not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Would you then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you or do you not know whether an act of terrorism is a criminal offence in Yugoslavia or was in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it is a criminal offence. I was just not sure which article of the criminal code covers it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope you mean myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, you would then agree with me that you would have to amend your answer to the previous questions that said that they were only duty-bound to protect the territory to include the fact that the MUP of Serbia was duty-bound by the obligations presented by the law to prosecute and to prevent terrorism by means available to it, would you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you understood that, but I would not amend my finding for the simple reason that I looked through the prism and focused on anti-terrorist combat and struggle, not the numerous tasks that the security forces had to perform by virtue of their very role. Of course that is implied, that's why I didn't deal with it specifically, but that formed the majority of tasks that every employee of the MUP had to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm focusing on the act of terrorism, which we've established was against the law, and I'd like to read for you a part of a document that as an expert in these matters I'm sure you have some familiarity with, Article 6 on the Law on Amending and supplementing the law on ministries. [Interpretation] Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, issue 44/91. [In English] -- 44/91, particularly section 3 of that act reads as for the duties of the MUP, this will be in B/C/S: [Interpretation] "Preventing and detecting criminal offences, apprehending perpetrators, and taking them into custody of the competent authorities." [In English] Would you agree with me that these duties of the MUP relate to every criminal act including terrorism and that the role of anti-terrorist activities is, in fact, dictated by the law.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The criminal offence of terrorism is certainly covered by what you said. It's not only about apprehension, though, because terrorists can usually not be apprehended because they offer armed resistance. They impose armed combat with the intention of inflicting losses. It's very difficult to apprehend them. In most cases, they are not apprehended because they can't be. They are neutralised by armed combat, they are broken up, and destroyed. Of course it would have been much better and more efficient if they could be apprehended and brought to trial like the perpetrators of other criminal offences; however, usually it doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to focus on the second part of your proposition in paragraph 90 of your report where you say that such a political decision predetermined that the crucial and leading role in that operation should be played by the police forces and police leadership. Now, in explaining the basis for your opinion in paragraph 91 you cite to the conclusions of the 9 June 1998 meeting of the Supreme Defence Council. Now, that is Exhibit P1574 which I would like to have up on the screen for purposes of allowing you to review the same. And I would ask you, sir: Am I correct that this document does not, in fact, have the conclusion that you state in paragraph 90, but in fact that this is a -- this is your interpretation of what is actually contained in P1574?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't make that conclusion only on the basis of this, of this document of the Supreme Defence Council. That conclusion of the Supreme Defence Council was in fact the basis for preparing the activities of defence forces. Such a conclusion on the decision not to introduce a state of emergency but do something else is based on many other insights from that time, the documents, and the developments that followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is that document also 4D138?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It may very well be, Your Honour. I don't have it noted as such, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're on paragraph 91, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's a different document that I'm about to get to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, right, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Indeed, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- At paragraph 91 you also cite to the Grom directive of General Perisic issued in 1998 as being another source for your conclusion on this. Would you agree with me then that General Perisic is an excellent source for describing the role of the various forces involved in anti-terrorist actions in 1998, as someone who actually participated in planning the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. If you're asking me whether General Perisic is the best person to talk to in terms of planning the role of the army, I agree on that; but as for other forces and other parts of the system, there were other organs that were in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, in support of your assertion in paragraph 90, you only cite to the conclusions of the 5th Session of the VSO and you talk about the directive for engagement of the VJ issued by General Perisic. I take it from that then you consider General Perisic as being a source for your conclusion that the police had a leading role in the operations of the anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is not an objection. I'm just trying to clarify where the document being referred to has been cited in paragraph 90 is in fact cited in paragraph 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't seem to be cited in paragraph 90 at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In 90 it's not. In 91 it's the Chief of the General Staff, of the Vojska Jugoslavije, General Perisic, pursuant to the conclusions of the fifth session of the VSO of 9 June, 1998, so he's basing in part his conclusion on the Perisic directive which is based on the VSO sessions so--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the conclusion is P1574, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the minutes of the meeting in question, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So that's how we get to -- from point A to point B.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The -- let me just see if the answer's been given. Sir, for the sake of clarity I will repeat the question that I had at page 87, line 10. In support of your assertion in paragraph 90, you only cite to the conclusions of the 5th Session of the VSO and you talk about the directive of the engagement of the VJ issued by General Perisic. I take it from that that you consider General Perisic as being a source for your conclusion that the police had a leading role in the operations of the anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I quoted General Perisic because in my report on -- focused on the role of the army and dealing with that. It goes without saying, if you look at the title of my report, that it pertains to the analysis of the control competence of General Ojdanic. And therefore, I focused on the army and the engagement of the army. As for the engagement of the army, I based that on the conclusions of the session of the Supreme Defence Council and its operational -- operation on General Perisic's decision on the 28th of July, 1998, giving the army the mandate to do that in line with that directive. So it's only that and it doesn't deal with other forces. I dealt with other forces only because there was something in common between that and what General Ojdanic did, the system of command of the army. As these are systems that exist along parallel lines, of course this did affect the functioning of the military. However, I did not go into detail as far as the MUP was concerned or civil protection or civil defence, except to the extent to which I concluded that they constitute a general context for the functioning of the army and General Ojdanic at the head of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude then, sir, that during your research and preparation for your expert testimony you did not, in fact, come across any order, either written or oral, from either the Serbian or Yugoslav leadership ordering the MUP of Serbia to carry the lead role and command anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not come across such an order, but it goes without saying from the role of the MUP in terms of providing security in the state, citizens, property, life in general, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can shift back to the VJ since that's the direction we seem to be going in, with respect to paragraph 90 you state that: "The army focused on securing the state border in-depth and military facilities of special importance and it provided logistic and fire support and assistance to the police forces which were the vehicle of anti-terrorist operations." Now, when you say that the VJ provided logistic and fire support for the police forces, can you be a bit more specific about what you mean, particularly with respect to fire support?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It is a generally understood thing. At the moment when the police forces are engaged in a blockade and destruction of terrorist strongholds, according to the law and in keeping with the coordination that existed on the ground the army is engaged to the extent to which it is asked to be engaged and to the extent to which it was possible under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would like to take a moment to look at Exhibit P1427 so that we can flush out the operations of these anti-terrorist actions a little bit more. Hopefully when this document comes up you will see that it is an "odluka." The B/C/S is up. I'm just waiting for the English, but I think I can proceed. First of all, sir, I presume that you--.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the benefit of those trying to follow the transcript, what is an "odluka"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was going to ask the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. No, ask the witness then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, could you describe the significance of an "odluka" in layman's terms? Is it a form of a decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: "Odluka", decision, in military terms, in military terminology is used in two senses. It can be a document, so it can be used as a document, and it can also be used as one of the points of an order of a commander for a particular action. And it is usually point 4, paragraph 4, of an order where he gives the corps of what he decided upon. So "odluka," decision, can be the fourth paragraph in the order of every commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Now, looking at this specific document, sir, and by all means, if you need to page through it we can have additional pages of the document shown to you. But would you agree with me that based upon the information presented in this decision or "odluka" the individual who drew up this document decided on the MUP and VJ being utilised in a joint action in August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to section 1 of this document, I would ask you doesn't in fact the text make clear that this is a joint action, not one being led by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Joint action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can move to section 2 which should be on the first page of both the B/C/S and the English, and also sections 2. -- Subsections 2.1 and 2.2 which should still be on that same page relating to fire support specifically. First of all, 2.1 speaks of supporting the attack as follows, and this is in B/C/S: [Interpretation] "BG-52 from the attained line supports the attack of the main forces OD MUP." [In English] Subsection 2.2 it is stated that the army will support the 9th Detachment of the MUP and PJP and SAJ, whereas subsection 3 says fire support as requested. Now, it would appear that different roles are being promulgated by this decision. Would you please comment on the tactical and functional differences between providing support for an attack, plane support, and if indeed this is more than just providing fire support, as the document would suggest?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at 2.1, the tasks of units, the person who made the decision, who decided, gives a task to combat group 52 to support the forces of the 2nd Detachment of the MUP. When he gives an order to support, that means that it is the MUP detachment that has the main task and the other one supports them, so that's auxiliary, otherwise it would be the other way around. He would say combat group 52 has a task and is supported by the MUP. This text leads to the obvious conclusion that it was the MUP that was protagonist of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, General, you haven't answered my question. Would you agree with me that under 2.1 and 2.2 the forces of the VJ are said to support the MUP, and such support is not limited to fire support. Is it not that they can also be used in manoeuvres with the MUP if the commander finds it necessary?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: There are different aspects of support. There is fire support, manoeuvre support, movement support, demonstration support, logistic support, through reconnaissance information, there can be different kinds of support, and indeed it is a broader concept than fire support on its own. You're right on that.
